<reason>Both sides were consistently sharp, well-referenced, and disciplined within the evidence rules. Side A's two strongest routes were the category/criterion dilemma (island category vs. risk logic) and the enforcement deficit (outvoted text has no teeth). Side B blunted both: the annihilation-vs-injury distinction gave a workable metric, and the closing reframe that every voting formula is chosen after its winner is known (population favors the populous, GDP the rich, consensus the powerful) turned the "rigging" charge into a weighing argument A never fully dismantished. On enforcement, B's comparative landed harder: consent under consensus has a thirty-year record of failure, the largest emitter quit Paris anyway, and agreed text creates baselines that courts, border adjustments, and finance conditions can bite on — while under consensus the ambitious text never exists to bite on at all. A's counter that those levers already exist today did not address that missing-text point. A's public-accountability counter (named blockers vs. quiet defiance) was real but narrow. B's "you demand guarantees of this reform that you never demand of the status quo" was the cleanest weighing move of the debate. Both asked effective pressure questions and answered A1/A2 squarely. A narrow but real edge to PRO on neutralizing CON's core attacks and winning the comparative on what the status quo actually delivers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over A's "rigging" charge: A argued in Rebuttal 2 that PRO's habitability-loss metric was reverse-engineered so Tuvalu outweighs Dhaka, "chosen after the desired winner was known." B's closing response — that population, GDP, and consensus formulas are all equally chosen to favor their beneficiaries, making survival-based weighting "the first honest one" — was the debate's most decisive reversal, converting A's sharpest attack into a reason to vote PRO.</best_rebuttal>
